verse_commentaries.commentary: LXX superscription inserts 'πρός τὸν Ἀσσύριον' (concerning the Assyrian) with zero basis in MT — earliest reception history already historicizing an otherwise unanchored hymn to Sennacherib's defeat.

lexical_insights.notes: Root נצח ambiguous: 'to oversee/direct' (musical) or 'perpetuity/enduring' — technical liturgical rubric of contested etymology, appears in 55 psalm headers.
From נגן 'play strings' — bare instrumental notation without accompanying tune-name (contrast Pss 22,45,56,60 which cite melody titles) — unusually minimal rubric.
Double genre-label 'psalm'+'song' co-occurs ~9x in Psalter (30,48,65-68,75,76,83,87,108); possible composite/intensified liturgical genre marker, not mere redundancy.
Absent from MT entirely. Later interpretive gloss tying psalm to Sennacherib narrative (2 Kgs 19//Isa 37); demonstrates earliest historicizing reception rather than textual variant.

verse_commentaries.commentary: Niphal נוֹדַע frames divine self-revelation as reflexive/passive event (God makes Himself known) rather than human discovery; Judah//Israel merism plus chiastic verb-noun placement encode totality of covenant nation.

lexical_insights.notes: Niphal perfect of ידע — reflexive-passive 'became known/made himself known,' subtly distinct from more agentive Hiphil הוֹדִיעַ; theological claim: revelation as divine self-disclosure, not human epistemic achievement.
Judah//Israel merism = whole covenant people; chiastic arrangement verb-location // adjective-location(reversed) creates envelope structure within single verse.
'Name theology' — שם as hypostasis of divine presence (cf. Deuteronomic 'name' theology, 1 Kgs 8); paired with נוֹדַע yields two-fold revelation register: personal (Elohim) + nominal (shem).

figurative_analysis: Name as extension/hypostasis of divine presence

verse_commentaries.commentary: LXX flattens שָׁלֵם into abstract 'ἐν εἰρήνη' (in peace), erasing the toponym Salem and its resonance with Melchizedek's city (Gen 14:18) — a striking interpretive loss of the place-name/peace paronomasia MT preserves.

lexical_insights.notes: Archaic Jerusalem toponym (Gen 14:18, king of Salem/Melchizedek), homophonous with שָׁלוֹם 'peace' — deliberate wordplay MT retains; LXX collapses toponym into abstract noun, losing the pun entirely.
From סֻכָּה 'booth/covert' — dual valence: cultic tabernacle-tent language AND thicket/lair for wild animal (cf. Job 38:40, lion's סֻכָּה) — ambiguity may be deliberate.

מְעוֹנָה = lion's den specifically (Amos 3:4, Nah 2:13, Ps 104:22) — combined with סוּכּוֹ constructs Zion as royal predator's lair, not gentle-shepherd dwelling; sets up harerei-taref (v5) predator continuation.

figurative_analysis: Zion/Salem as lion's den — predator metaphor for divine habitation

verse_commentaries.commentary: רִשְׁפֵי־קֶשֶׁת likely echoes Resheph, Canaanite plague/war deity, subtly demythologized into mere 'fiery arrows'; weapon-triad shield→sword→war escalates from concrete to abstract, as if God dismantles the very concept of war.

lexical_insights.notes: רֶשֶׁף = flame/spark/plague, also name of Canaanite deity of plague/lightning/war (Ugaritic, Phoenician; cf. Hab 3:5, Deut 32:24) — possible mythological substrate demythologized as poetic imagery. LXX 'τὸ κράτος τοῦ τόξου' (might of the bow) avoids fire-imagery, suggests translational flattening or differing reading.

Locative 'there,' resumes deictic pointer to Zion (v3); creates spatial anchor contrasted with מִשָּׁמַיִם 'from heaven' (v9) — 'there/from-heaven' dialectic structures psalm's vertical-horizontal geography.

Triad shield>sword>war(abstract) — synecdochic escalation from specific defensive/offensive weapons to the totalizing abstraction 'war' itself; merism signals complete disarmament, not partial victory.

figurative_analysis: Weapons personified/shattered by divine hand; possible echo of storm-god smashing enemy arms (Baal Cycle parallel)
verse_commentaries.phonetic_transcription: SHĀM-māh shib-BAR rish-fēy-QĀ-sheth mā-GHĒN wə-ḤE-rev ū-mil-ḥā-MĀH SE-lāh

verse_commentaries.commentary: Text-critical crux: MT הַרְרֵי־טֶרֶף ('mountains of prey/torn-flesh') vs LXX ὄρος αἰώνιος ('eternal mountain'), implying Vorlage הַרְרֵי־עַד — did LXX soften violent predator imagery or preserve authentic variant harmonized to the stock phrase in Deut 33:15/Hab 3:6?

lexical_insights.notes: Rare Niphal participle from אור 'light' — 'resplendent/luminous,' near-hapax form; theophanic light-language paralleling divine kavod traditions.
Emphatic 2ms pronoun anticipates doubled אַתָּה...אַתָּה of v8 — first half of paired direct-address structure bracketing theophanic assertions.

טֶרֶף = prey/torn flesh (predator's kill) continuing lion-den imagery from v3 מְעוֹנָתוֹ. LXX ὄρος αἰώνιος implies alternate reading הַרְרֵי־עַד ('ancient/everlasting mountains,' cf. Hab 3:6, Deut 33:15) — genuine text-critical question, not mere translation choice.

figurative_analysis: God as luminous predator on 'mountains of prey' — continued lion imagery

verse_commentaries.commentary: LXX's 'πᾶς ὁ ἀσύνετος τῇ καρδίᾳ' (all senseless in heart) nearly inverts MT's אַבִּירֵי לֵב ('mighty/valiant of heart') — striking semantic reversal suggesting divergent Vorlage or deliberate ironic recasting of warrior-pride as folly.

lexical_insights.notes: Rare Eshtaphel/Hitpael of שלל 'to plunder' — reflexive-passive 'they were despoiled,' unusual verbal stem (possible Aramaic influence); irony: elite plunderers become plundered.
Idiom 'mighty/stout of heart' = elite warriors; LXX's ἀσύνετος (senseless/foolish) diverges sharply — possible alternate root reading or deliberate reversal for polemical effect.
Cognate accusative 'slept their sleep' — rare root נום (cf. Isa 5:27, Nah 3:18); death-sleep euphemism continuing paralysis motif.
Idiom for utter incapacity/helplessness; 'hands' = agency/instrument motif, victory achieved without human counter-action.

figurative_analysis: Warriors reduced to sleep/stupor — divine victory via paralysis, not combat
verse_commentaries.phonetic_transcription: 'esh-tō-lə-LŪ 'ab-BIY-rēy LĒV nā-MŪ shə-nā-THĀM wə-lō'-mā-tsə-'Ū khol-'an-shēy-ḤA-yil yə-dhēy-HEM

verse_commentaries.commentary: מִגַּעֲרָתְךָ invokes the classic Divine-Warrior rebuke that elsewhere quells cosmic chaos-waters (Ps 18:16, 104:7) — here retargeted at horse and chariot, collapsing mythic Chaoskampf into historicized battle report.

lexical_insights.notes: גערה 'rebuke/roar/blast' — stock Divine-Warrior motif, typically directed at chaotic sea/waters (Ps 18:16, 104:7, Isa 50:2, Nah 1:4); here redirected onto cavalry, historicizing cosmic imagery.
Niphal רדם 'stunned/deep-sleep' — distinct root from v6's נָמוּ but same death-sleep semantic field; stacked near-synonyms across vv6-7 intensify paralysis theme.
Patriarchal epithet, unique in this Elohistic psalm; 'Jacob' evokes wrestling narrative (Gen 32) — ironic given enemies here cannot even struggle.
Order chariot-then-horse reverses more common סוּס וָרֶכֶב (Ex 15:1, Ps 20:8) — possibly metrical or deliberate variation.

figurative_analysis: Horse and chariot personified, falling stunned at mere sound of divine rebuke

verse_commentaries.commentary: Doubled אַתָּה...אַתָּה sandwiching נוֹרָא is rare emphatic syntax ('You! Awesome! You!'), the psalm's strongest self-referential assertion of incomparability, paired with the puzzlingly vague temporal marker מֵאָז whose referent is left undefined.

lexical_insights.notes: Doubled 2ms pronoun bracketing predicate adjective — rare BH syntax, doubling for maximal emphasis; נוֹרָא (Niphal ptc. of ירא) launches the fear-root chain saturating vv8-13 (nora/yir'ah/mora/nora).
Rhetorical-question formula, cf. Nah 1:6, Mal 3:2, Ps 130:3 — stock Divine-Warrior/theodicy device asserting unassailability.
אָז 'then/at that time' — unclear referent (creation? Exodus? present battle?); genuinely ambiguous temporal anchor for onset of divine wrath.

verse_commentaries.commentary: Possible paronomasia between מִשָּׁמַיִם ('from heaven') and הִשְׁמַעְתָּ ('you caused to be heard') via shared ש-מ consonants sonically links heaven and speech; earth's fear resolves paradoxically into stillness (שָׁקְטָה) rather than chaos.

lexical_insights.notes: Heaven as locus of the דִּין-verdict; spatial pivot from local 'there' (Zion, v4) to cosmic 'from heaven' — universalizes the earlier military victory into cosmic tribunal.
דִּין = juridical 'verdict/sentence,' rarer/more technical term than מִשְׁפָּט (v10); Hiphil 'caused to be heard' = formal proclamation, courtroom register. Possible ש-מ paronomasia with מִשָּׁמַיִם.
Earth personified: ירא 'fear' (launches fear-root inclusio) + שקט 'be quiet/still' (cf. Josh 11:23 'land had rest'); paradox — terror yields stillness, not flight or chaos.

figurative_analysis: Earth personified as terrified, subdued into silence

verse_commentaries.commentary: Pairing of דִּין (v9, sentence pronounced) with מִשְׁפָּט (v10, judgment executed) suggests deliberate two-stage forensic sequence — heavenly verdict then earthly enactment — and the stated purpose לְהוֹשִׁיעַ עַנְוֵי־אֶרֶץ reframes cosmic wrath entirely as salvation for the oppressed.

lexical_insights.notes: קום 'arise' — stock Divine-Warrior battle-mobilization formula (Num 10:35 'קוּמָה ה׳'); here fused with judicial מִשְׁפָּט, blending martial and forensic registers.
Hiphil infinitive purpose clause — salvation is judgment's telos, not incidental byproduct; central to Asaphite social-justice theology.
עָנָו 'lowly/humble/afflicted' — social-justice term (cf. Ps 37:11, Isa 11:4). Third אֶרֶץ occurrence in three verses (v9x2, v10) — repetition drums heaven-earth linkage.

verse_commentaries.commentary: Major interpretive crux: MT's paradox 'wrath of man shall praise you / remnant of wraths you gird' diverges radically from LXX's 'thought of man shall confess... remnant of thought shall keep festival' — likely reflecting root-confusion (חגר 'gird' vs חגג 'celebrate') or a wholly different reading tradition; the polyptoton חֲמַת/חֵמֹת (same root, singular/plural) is deliberate wordplay regardless.

lexical_insights.notes: Paradox: 'wrath of man praises/acknowledges you' (תּוֹדֶךָּ from ידה, Hiphil 'confess/praise') — human hostility co-opted into doxology; unclear mechanism — does defeat convert rage into confession, or does surviving wrath merely testify involuntarily to God's supremacy?

תַּחְגֹּר 'you gird on' (חגר, military belt/weapon idiom) — obscure image of God arming/adorning himself with leftover wrath as trophy. LXX ἑορτάσει ('will keep festival') implies root חגג not חגר — significant textual/translational crux, possibly ר/ג confusion or independent tradition.
Polyptoton — same root ח.מ.ה 'heat/wrath' in construct singular then plural — deliberate repetition/intensification device.

figurative_analysis: Divine warrior girding on leftover human wrath as ornament/trophy-weapon

verse_commentaries.commentary: לַמּוֹרָא is a striking nominalized divine epithet ('to the Awesome One'), climaxing the fear-root chain (נורא v8/13, יראה v9) as a formal divine title — yet LXX curiously relocates/omits it, shifting φοβερός to open v13 instead, revealing verse-division divergence between MT and LXX traditions.

lexical_insights.notes: Paired imperatives 'vow, pay' — stock cultic-legal formula (cf. Eccl 5:3-4, Deut 23:22) on fulfilling vows; alliterative נ/ש consonance.

מוֹרָא 'fear/awe' nominalized with definite article as divine title 'the Awesome One' — rare substantivized usage (cf. Deut 26:8 'מוֹרָא גָּדוֹל' of Exodus terror, but not elsewhere as direct epithet); climactic node of fear-root inclusio.
'All around him' — ambiguous referent: heavenly divine council (cf. Ps 89:8) or earthly vassal-nations bringing tribute; possible deliberate double-register.
שַׁי rare noun 'tribute/gift' (only Ps 68:30, Isa 18:7, here) — royal-court vocabulary; reinforces YHWH-as-cosmic-suzerain motif receiving vassal tribute.

figurative_analysis: YHWH as cosmic king/suzerain receiving vassal tribute
verse_commentaries.phonetic_transcription: nidh-RŪ wə-shal-lə-MŪ lay-hō-WĀH 'e-lō-hēy-KHEM kol-sə-viy-VĀYW yō-VIY-lū SHAY lam-mō-RĀ'

verse_commentaries.commentary: יִבְצֹר derives from a viticultural root ('prune/cut off grapes') applied metaphorically to political power — striking agricultural image for deflating royal pride, with genuine ambiguity against the homonymous root בצר II ('fortify/restrain'); final נוֹרָא closes the fear-root inclusio opened at v8.

lexical_insights.notes: Root ambiguity: בצר I 'cut off/prune/harvest grapes' vs בצר II 'be inaccessible/fortified' (cf. בְּצוּרָה fortified city) — does God 'prune/cut short' princely spirit (harvest metaphor) or 'restrain/wall it off' (fortification metaphor)? LXX ἀφαιρέω ('take away') leans toward the cutting sense.
נָגִיד — specific term for divinely-designated ruler (Saul/David pre-monarchic anointing, 1 Sam 9:16, 13:14); politically loaded term subjected to divine pruning.
Final נוֹרָא occurrence closes inclusio with v8, bracketing entire second half with the 'awesome' root; 'kings of the earth' universalizing climax (cf. Ps 2:2,10 hostile kings, now submissive).

figurative_analysis: God as vinedresser pruning royal pride like grapevines — harvest metaphor for political subjugation

interesting_questions: Why does LXX insert 'πρός τὸν Ἀσσύριον' in the superscription (v1) when MT contains no historical referent at all — what triggered this specific historicization to Sennacherib?
Is LXX's 'ἐν εἰρήνη' for שָׁלֵם (v3) a deliberate erasure of the toponym Salem, severing the psalm's link to Melchizedek traditions (Gen 14:18) and the peace/place-name paronomasia?
Does רִשְׁפֵי־קֶשֶׁת (v4) preserve mythological substrate referencing the Canaanite plague-deity Resheph, and how thoroughly has the psalmist demythologized it into mere 'fiery arrows'?
Is MT's הַרְרֵי־טֶרֶף ('mountains of prey,' v5) original, or does LXX's ὄρος αἰώνιος reflect a genuine alternate Vorlage הַרְרֵי־עַד (cf. Deut 33:15, Hab 3:6)?

Why does LXX v6 render אַבִּירֵי לֵב ('stout-hearted') as ἀσύνετος τῇ καρδίᾳ ('senseless-hearted') — an apparent semantic inversion — reflecting a different Vorlage, ironic recasting, or theological polemic against warrior pride?
What is the referent of the enigmatic temporal marker מֵאָז ('from then,' v8) — creation, Exodus, or the immediate battle context?
How does the pairing of דִּין (v9, sentence pronounced) and מִשְׁפָּט (v10, judgment executed) map onto a deliberate two-stage forensic sequence — heavenly verdict then earthly enactment?
What mechanism does חֲמַת אָדָם תּוֹדֶךָּ (v11) envision — does defeated human wrath literally transmute into confession/praise, or is this ironic/coerced acknowledgment of superior power?

Is LXX's rendering of v11's תַּחְגֹּר ('gird') as ἑορτάσει ('celebrate a festival') evidence of root confusion (חגר vs חגג) or an independent interpretive tradition — and what does this crux do to the verse's martial imagery?

Does יִבְצֹר (v13) intend the viticultural sense ('prune/cut off,' per LXX ἀφαιρέω) or the fortification sense ('restrain/confine'), and how does this root-ambiguity shape the metaphor for divine control over princely 'spirit'?
Why does the fear-root cluster (ירא/נורא/מורא) appear nowhere in vv2-7 yet saturate vv8-13 — marking a clear structural/rhetorical break within the psalm?

Why are סוּכּוֹ (cultic 'booth') and מְעוֹנָתוֹ ('lion's den') paired in v3 — what does juxtaposing tabernacle-language with predator-lair language suggest about the poet's theology of divine dwelling?
